questions.source: Gate — subnetting archetype (recycles in every paper)
questions.prompt: **10.130.73.95/27** — give the **network address** of this subnet.
questions.explain: /27 ⇒ block size 32 in the last octet (256−224). Blocks: 0, 32, **64**, 96… 95 sits in the 64-block → network **10.130.73.64**, broadcast **.95**.

questions.prompt: **192.168.4.0/24** split into 4 equal subnets. Give the **broadcast address of Subnet 2** (the third subnet).

questions.source: Gate — fragmentation table (Tier-1 archetype, appears in nearly every paper)
questions.prompt: A **4000-byte** datagram (20-byte header) must cross a link with **MTU 1500**. Which fragmentation table is correct? (offsets in 8-byte units)
options: 3 fragments: lengths 1500/1500/1040 · offsets 0/185/370 · flags 1/1/0
3 fragments: lengths 1500/1500/1000 · offsets 0/1500/3000 · flags 1/1/0
3 fragments: lengths 1480/1480/1020 · offsets 0/185/370 · flags 0/0/1
2 fragments: lengths 1500/2500 · offsets 0/185 · flags 1/0
questions.explain:
Data to carry = 4000−20 = **3980 bytes**; each fragment carries ≤ 1500−20 = **1480** data bytes.

| Frag | Total len | Data | Offset (×8 bytes) | Flag (more?) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1500 | 1480 | **0** | 1 |
| 2 | 1500 | 1480 | 1480/8 = **185** | 1 |
| 3 | 1020+20=**1040** | 1020 | 2960/8 = **370** | **0** |

Every fragment gets a full 20-byte IP header; offset counts DATA bytes in 8-byte units; last fragment's flag = 0.

questions.prompt: Put the **DHCP** message exchange in order (client obtaining an address):
questions.explain: **D-O-R-A**: Discover → Offer → Request → ACK. Runs over **UDP** (ports 67/68); Discover and Request are broadcast because the client has no usable IP yet. DHCP can also hand out the mask, default gateway, and DNS server ('plug-and-play').

questions.prompt: Which field(s) does a NAT router rewrite for an **outgoing** datagram from a private host?
options: Source IP and source port (to its WAN IP + a fresh port), recorded in the NAT table
Destination IP and destination port
Only the source IP; ports never change
Source MAC address only
questions.explain: Outgoing: (src IP:port) → (**NAT WAN IP : new port**), one row per connection in the translation table. Replies arriving at that WAN port are mapped back to the private (IP:port). Destination fields are untouched.

questions.source: Gate — stealth marks: routing algorithms (3 of last 4 finals!)
questions.prompt: **Dijkstra's** algorithm, as used by OSPF, is best described as:
options: A LINK-STATE algorithm: every router knows the full topology and computes least-cost paths from itself
A DISTANCE-VECTOR algorithm: routers only know their neighbours' estimates
A flooding algorithm with no cost metric
A spanning-tree algorithm for switches
questions.explain:
**Link state (Dijkstra/OSPF):** global knowledge — each router floods link costs, then computes shortest paths itself; after k iterations, k nodes have final least-cost paths.
**Distance vector (Bellman-Ford/RIP):** iterative, distributed — each router only exchanges estimates with neighbours: Dx(y) = min over v { c(x,v) + Dv(y) }.
Not on the weekly schedule — but appeared in 3 of the last 4 written finals (6–20 marks).

questions.source: Gate — stealth marks: distance vector pathology
questions.prompt: The **count-to-infinity** problem affects which algorithm, and what is the classic mitigation?
options: Distance vector — poisoned reverse (advertise infinite cost back through the path you use)
Link state — flooding suppression
Distance vector — increasing the hello interval
Link state — splitting the area into subnets
questions.explain: When a link cost INCREASES, distance-vector routers can bounce wrong estimates between each other ('good news travels fast, **bad news travels slow**'). **Poisoned reverse**: if Z routes to X via Y, Z tells Y its distance to X is ∞ — breaking 2-node loops (not all larger loops).

questions.prompt: Which row of IPv4→IPv6 changes is fully correct?
options: 128-bit addresses · fixed 40-byte header · NO router fragmentation · NO header checksum
64-bit addresses · variable header · routers fragment · keeps checksum
128-bit addresses · keeps options in base header · routers fragment · keeps checksum
96-bit addresses · 20-byte header · no fragmentation · adds checksum
questions.explain: IPv6: **128-bit** addresses, streamlined **fixed 40-byte** header, **no fragmentation by routers** (sender gets ICMP 'packet too big'), **no checksum** (done at transport/link), flow label added. Transition: **tunneling** — IPv6 datagram carried as payload inside IPv4 between IPv6 islands.

questions.prompt: A forwarding table holds `200.23.16.0/20 → if0` and `200.23.24.0/21 → if1` and default → if2. Where does **200.23.26.77** go?
options: if1 — /21 is the longest matching prefix
if0 — /20 matches first in the table
if2 — no entry matches
if0 and if1 — load balanced
questions.explain: 26 is inside 24–31 (the /21 block 200.23.24.0–200.23.31.255) AND inside 16–31 (the /20). Both match → **longest prefix (/21) wins → if1**. Write the method sentence: 'the entry with the longest address prefix that matches the destination address is selected.'

questions.prompt: VLSM from **192.168.10.0/24**, largest first: HR 50 → /26, IT 30 → /27, Sales 20 → /27, Mgmt 10 → /28. What is the **network address of the Sales subnet**?
questions.explain:
Sequential largest-first allocation:
HR /26 → .0 (ends .63) · IT /27 → .64 (ends .95) · **Sales /27 → .96** (ends .127) · Mgmt /28 → .128 (ends .143).
Each subnet starts where the previous block ends, aligned to its own block size.

questions.prompt: Which IPv4 header field is **decremented by each router**, and what happens at 0?
options: TTL — datagram is discarded and an ICMP time-exceeded is sent back
Checksum — datagram is re-verified
Fragment offset — datagram is reassembled
Identification — datagram is renumbered
questions.explain: **TTL (time-to-live)** drops by 1 per hop → at 0 the router discards the datagram and returns **ICMP time exceeded** (this is how *traceroute* works). The checksum is recomputed each hop because TTL changed.

questions.prompt: A subnet must host **500** devices. How many **host bits** are required?
questions.explain: 500 + 2 ≤ 2⁹ = 512 ⇒ **9 host bits** (prefix /23, 510 usable). 2⁸ = 256 is too small once network + broadcast are subtracted.
